aiSummary: Speckled trout and bull redfish are the top targets across Choctawhatchee Bay right now, with a recent report noting plenty of trout in the bay alongside large bull reds — one measuring over 40 inches. At 86°F, water temps are pushing trout toward early-morning and dusk windows, so a dawn start will be critical before the heat shuts things down. A 34% storm chance before 4 PM adds urgency to wrapping up on exposed water by midday, though protected bayous offer a safer fallback if weather builds.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel that pushes bait through on both tides. Pilings hold speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with lee-side pilings serving as the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. Being open water, this is typically the first spot to become unfishable when wind picks up or weather builds.
bridge.todaysCall: The low tide at 12:39 PM means the incoming tide push will be building through the morning — work the lee-side pilings early as current accelerates and bait funnels through. With ESE winds at only 5 mph, chop should be manageable at first light, but the 34% storm chance before 4 PM means plan to be off this exposed water by late morning. Slightly stained water actually helps here — trout and reds will be tighter to the pilings and less spooky. Hit it at first light (sunrise 6:05 AM) and fish hard through the early incoming push before heat and storm risk build.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou is a protected fishery with a strong year-round redfish population, plus speckled trout and flounder at the mouth. Oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime structural element, and tree cover keeps the interior a few degrees cooler than the open bay while offering shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish water and holds bass alongside smaller redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: Tree cover and protected orientation make Alaqua a smart call today given the storm chance before 4 PM — you can fish longer here than on open water without feeling boxed in by weather. Work the oyster bars at the mouth on the building incoming tide after the 12:39 PM low, but your best window for trout is early morning before water temps climb from 86°F. The slightly stained water suits redfish well — they'll be hunting the oyster structure by feel and vibration, so noisy or dark-colored lures and cut bait are solid choices. Bull reds have been active bay-wide, so don't ignore the creek mouth on the tide change.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less fishing pressure than Alaqua and LaGrange, meaning the fish here tend to be less educated. Interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water, and pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It is less protected than LaGrange when weather builds, so keep that in mind if conditions deteriorate.
basin.todaysCall: Less-pressured fish are a real advantage today when the bite window is compressed by 86°F water temps — get on the interior grass flats at first light and look for reds in the skinny water before the sun climbs. The slightly stained water reduces sight-fishing quality somewhat, so lean on noise and scent rather than purely visual presentations. With a storm chance before 4 PM and Basin offering less weather protection than LaGrange, commit to an early start and plan your exit — be back at the ramp well before noon if clouds start stacking. The incoming tide building after the 12:39 PM low is a secondary window, but the heat and storm timing make the morning push the priority.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer in this bay system, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside the bayou hold black drum and sheepshead, rounding out the species mix. It is the most protected water on this side of the bay, making it the go-to location when weather threatens.
lagrange.todaysCall: This is the strongest all-around pick for today — the protection from building weather, the proven trout-and-redfish bite, and the structural variety all line up well. Hit the oyster bars at the mouth at first light (sunrise 6:05 AM) while trout are still active in the cooler morning temps; 86°F water is pushing them toward low-light windows. Slightly stained water won't hurt LaGrange's oyster-bar fishing — reds and drum work by feel along hard structure regardless of clarity. The incoming tide building after the 12:39 PM low will fire up the mouth again later in the day, but with the storm window running before 4 PM, the morning session is the play — stay protected and let the weather pass before deciding on an afternoon round.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where tidal flow pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates redfish and trout in the bends and grass edges. The creek mouth is a prime flounder zone, and the upper section transitions toward brackish water with bass alongside smaller reds. It is a short, protected fishery and one of the safest options when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is an excellent choice today precisely because of the storm risk — short, enclosed, and easy to exit quickly if lightning becomes a concern before 4 PM. The incoming tide building after the 12:39 PM low will push baitfish up the bends, so position in a creek bend or grass edge ahead of that push. Early morning is still the priority window given 86°F water temps, so fish the mouth and lower bends at first light for trout, then work up the creek as the tide turns. The slight stain in the water is no obstacle here — this creek fishes well on scent and presentation, and the naturally narrower channel keeps fish concentrated.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination and one of the most productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay. Summer mornings are the peak period, with trout stacked on grass in two to four feet of water, and Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides. It sees regular pressure but produces consistently, though its location further from the 331 Bridge means factoring in additional run time.
hogtown.todaysCall: The morning window is absolutely critical at Hogtown today — 86°F water temps mean trout on the grass flats will be most active right around sunrise (6:05 AM) and will shut down as the sun climbs. Plan your run time accordingly so you're rigged and on the flat at first light rather than arriving late. Spanish mackerel at the mouth are worth a few casts on the early tide movement, but trout on the interior grass in 2–4 feet is the primary target. Factor the storm window (before 4 PM) and the longer return run into your exit plan — Hogtown is not the place to be caught napping when afternoon thunder starts building on the horizon.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou, the top trout producer in this bay system, just south of Freeport. That direct connection means LaGrange's proven oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern plausibly extends into this smaller, quieter water, though documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou itself is limited. Its small, interior character makes it a natural calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: If LaGrange Bayou's mouth is crowded or you want a quieter alternative, Mallet is worth exploring today — its direct connection to LaGrange makes the same redfish and trout patterns at least plausible. Fish it early, as 86°F water temps compress the active window to low-light hours. The slight stain and interior position won't hurt — in tight, shallow water, reds especially respond well to scent and noise regardless of clarity. Treat it as a secondary stop rather than a primary destination, and note that the storm risk before 4 PM is actually less threatening here given how sheltered and quickly exitable this small interior water is.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a long-run destination rather than a quick local trip. It shares protected-bayou character with Alaqua and LaGrange, featuring marsh grass, oyster bars, and a few interior holes, and sees less pressure simply due to its distance from main boat ramps. Hewett and Buck Bayous sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: The long run to Mack Bayou is the main consideration today — with a 34% storm chance before 4 PM, make sure you're comfortable with the open-bay crossing in both directions and have a clear exit strategy. Depart well before sunrise so you're fishing at first light (6:05 AM) when trout are most active at 86°F water temps. Less pressure here means less-educated fish, which is a genuine advantage when the bite window is tight. Pair it with Hewett and/or Buck to make the run worthwhile, and keep a close eye on the western sky — afternoon storms on this side of the bay can build fast.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, and pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou in the same trip. Like its neighbors, it offers protected-bayou habitat with oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth and deeper interior holes further in. Light pressure due to its distance from the main boat ramps keeps fish less conditioned to lures.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett is best approached as part of a Mack-Hewett combo run today — the long crossing from the 331 Bridge area demands you make the most of the trip, and these two spots share the same habitat and species mix. Get on the water before sunrise to cover the crossing and be fishing by 6:05 AM; 86°F water means the trout bite on the oyster-bar and grass-edge structure will be sharpest in the first two hours of light. The storm risk before 4 PM is a firm deadline — plan your return crossing to be completed well before that window, as open-bay runs in building afternoon weather are not where you want to be. Slightly stained water and light pressure favor your odds at both spots.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak confidently about it. It is best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck makes sense today only as a quick bonus stop after hitting Mack and Hewett — don't build your whole trip around it given the limited documentation and the storm clock running before 4 PM. If you're already in the neighborhood and have time before conditions build, a few exploratory casts along the oyster structure and grass edges could turn up reds or trout that have escaped pressure at the larger neighbors. Keep the visit short and stay aware of your return-run timing — the open-bay crossing back toward the 331 Bridge in building afternoon weather is the real risk management consideration for this whole western trip.
